schengen.name: Schengen Visa 90/180 Day Calculator
schengen.metaTitle: Schengen 90/180 Day Calculator — Rolling Window Visa Tracker
schengen.metaDescription: Track your Schengen short-stay allowance with the official rolling 180-day rule. Add every trip, see days used, days remaining, overstay warnings and your next legal entry date.
schengen.intro: Add your past and planned trips to see exactly how many of your 90 days remain inside the rolling 180-day window — and the earliest date you can legally re-enter.
features: Rolling 180-day window evaluated day by day
Overstay detection with exact excess days
Next legal entry date and maximum consecutive stay

ui.referenceDateHint: The day you want to be assessed on — usually today or a planned entry date.
ui.tripsHint: Entry and exit days both count as full days of presence.
ui.statusOkBody: You are within the 90/180 allowance on the reference date.
ui.statusWarningBody: You have used more than 80% of your allowance. Plan the next entry carefully.
ui.statusCriticalBody: No days left on this date. You must wait until the window rolls forward.
ui.statusOverstayBody: Your itinerary breaches the 90-day limit by {days} day(s). Adjust the trips before travelling.
ui.violationDetail: {date}: {days} days in the preceding 180-day window ({excess} over the limit)
ui.reversedRange: Exit date must not be before the entry date
ui.noTrips: Add your first trip to see the calculation.
ui.timelineHint: Days of presence counted for each day of the last 180 days.

formula.intro: The short-stay rule comes from Article 6 of the Schengen Borders Code: a maximum of 90 days of presence in any 180-day period. The window is not a fixed calendar block — it rolls forward one day at a time.
steps: Pick the reference date D (today, or the day you plan to enter).
Build the window: the 180 consecutive days ending on D, i.e. [D − 179, D].
Count every day of physical presence inside that window. Entry day and exit day each count as one full day.
Overlapping trips are counted once — a day is either spent inside the area or it is not.
Days remaining = 90 − days counted. A negative result is an overstay.
For the next legal entry, step forward day by day until the window contains 89 days or fewer.
formula.note: This tool models the rule itself. Long-stay national visas, residence permits and bilateral exemptions can change how days are counted — always confirm with the consulate of your destination.

sections.heading: What the 90/180 rule actually means
paragraphs: Most visa-exempt travellers and holders of a short-stay Schengen visa may spend up to 90 days in the Schengen area within any 180-day period. The frequent misunderstanding is that the 180 days reset on a fixed date, or that leaving the area starts a fresh count. Neither is true.

The window is retrospective and rolling: on any given day, a border officer looks back 179 days plus the current day and adds up your days of presence. That is why an itinerary that felt legal in March can become an overstay in May without you spending a single extra day abroad.

sections.heading: How days are counted at the border
paragraphs: The day you enter counts as a whole day, even if you land at 23:50. The day you leave counts as a whole day too, even for an early-morning flight. A weekend trip from Friday to Sunday therefore consumes three days, not two.

Transit through a Schengen airport without crossing into the area does not normally count, but any passport stamp on entry does. Keep boarding passes and stamps: if the count is disputed, the burden of proof is on the traveller.
list: Entry day and exit day are both full days.
Consecutive trips separated by a day still count each individual day of presence.
The count covers all Schengen states together, not per country.
Time on a long-stay national visa or residence permit is normally excluded from the 90-day pot.

sections.heading: Consequences of an overstay
paragraphs: Penalties range from a warning stamp to a fine, a removal order or an entry ban recorded in the SIS database for up to several years. Even a short overstay can complicate future visa applications, residence permits and Schengen entries.

If you discover that a planned itinerary breaches the limit, adjust it before departure. Once you are inside the area, options narrow to a national extension request, which is granted only for force majeure or humanitarian reasons.

sections.heading: Planning trips around the rolling window
paragraphs: The practical strategy is to plan backwards from the day you want to enter. Enter your planned trip in this calculator, set the reference date to the intended entry day, and check that the window still has room for the whole stay.

If the allowance is exhausted, the tool reports the first date on which a new entry becomes legal and how many consecutive days would then be available. From that date on, the allowance regenerates day by day as older stays drop out of the window.

faq.question: Does the 180-day period reset every six months?
faq.answer: No. It is a rolling window, recalculated every single day. On any given date the authorities look back over the previous 180 days, including that date, and count your days of presence. There is no fixed reset date.

faq.question: Do the entry and exit days both count?
faq.answer: Yes. Both are counted as full days regardless of the time of day. A trip from 1 June to 3 June uses three days of your allowance.

faq.question: What happens if I have already overstayed?
faq.answer: Possible consequences include a fine, an obligation to leave, a removal decision or an entry ban registered in the Schengen Information System. Contact the immigration authority of the country you are in before your situation worsens, and expect closer scrutiny on future applications.

faq.question: Are Ireland, Bulgaria, Romania or Cyprus included?
faq.answer: Ireland is not part of the Schengen area and applies its own rules. Bulgaria and Romania joined the Schengen area for air and sea borders in 2024 and for land borders in 2025, so recent stays there do count. Cyprus is still outside the area. Always verify the current status before relying on old advice.

faq.question: Does a residence permit or long-stay visa consume my 90 days?
faq.answer: Normally no. Time spent in the issuing country under a national long-stay visa (type D) or a residence permit is not deducted from the 90/180 short-stay allowance. Time spent in other Schengen states may still count, so check the terms of your permit.

faq.question: Is my trip data stored anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser, and trip dates never leave your device. Reloading the page clears everything unless you save it yourself.

fire.name: FIRE & Compound Interest Calculator
fire.metaTitle: FIRE Calculator — Compound Interest with Inflation Adjustment
fire.metaDescription: Project your path to financial independence: monthly contributions, compound growth, inflation-adjusted purchasing power, the 4% rule and the exact age your portfolio covers your expenses.
fire.intro: Model monthly investing with compound growth, salary increases and inflation, then see the age at which your portfolio can safely cover your annual spending.
features: Monthly compounding with annual contribution growth
FIRE number from any safe withdrawal rate
Year-by-year growth chart and data table

ui.fireNumberHint: Annual spending ÷ withdrawal rate, in today's money.
ui.onTrack: On track for your target age
ui.growthShare: {percent}% of the final portfolio comes from compounding
ui.requiredContribution: Monthly saving needed to hit the target on time

formula.intro: The projection compounds monthly and separates nominal currency from real purchasing power, because a portfolio that doubles while prices double has not made you richer.
steps: Convert the annual return r into a monthly rate: rm = (1 + r)^(1/12) − 1.
For every month: balance = balance × (1 + rm) + contribution.
Increase the contribution once per year by the salary-growth rate.
Deflate the balance to today's money: real = nominal ÷ (1 + i)^years, where i is inflation.
FIRE number = annual spending ÷ safe withdrawal rate (4% → 25× spending).
Inflate the target forward each year and report the first year the nominal balance clears it.
formula.note: Returns are modelled as a smooth average. Real markets are volatile and sequence-of-returns risk matters in the first years of withdrawal — treat the output as a planning baseline, not a promise.

sections.heading: Why compounding beats contribution size over time
paragraphs: In the first years, almost all portfolio growth comes from the money you deposit. Somewhere between year ten and year fifteen — depending on the return you assume — the annual gain produced by the portfolio itself overtakes the annual contribution. From that point on, time in the market matters more than the size of each deposit.
This is why the chart shows contributions and total balance separately: the gap between the two lines is the part of your wealth that compounding built for you.

sections.heading: Reading the 4% rule correctly
paragraphs: The 4% safe withdrawal rate comes from the Trinity study and its successors, which tested historical 30-year retirements against a portfolio of stocks and bonds. It implies a FIRE number of roughly 25 times annual spending.

It is a heuristic, not a law. Longer retirements, lower expected returns, high fees or an early bear market all argue for a lower rate — 3.25% to 3.5% is a common conservative choice, which raises the target to roughly 29–31 times spending.
list: 5.0% → 20× annual spending, but with materially higher depletion risk

sections.heading: Inflation is the quiet variable
paragraphs: At 2.5% inflation, prices roughly double in 28 years. A portfolio target set in today's money must therefore be inflated to the year you actually retire, otherwise you will hit a nominal number that no longer buys the life you planned.
The calculator does both: the nominal line shows the balance you will literally see in your account, and the real line shows what it is worth in the prices you know today.

faq.question: What return rate should I assume?
faq.answer: A globally diversified equity portfolio has historically returned about 7–8% nominal per year over long periods, before fees. Many planners use 5–6% for a mixed portfolio, or subtract inflation and work in real terms. Lower assumptions produce plans that are harder to break.

faq.question: Should I enter numbers before or after inflation?
faq.answer: Enter the nominal return and inflation separately, and set your spending in today's money. The calculator inflates the target and shows both nominal and real balances, so you never have to mix the two conventions yourself.

faq.question: How is the FIRE number calculated?
faq.answer: FIRE number = annual spending ÷ (withdrawal rate ÷ 100). With 30,000 of annual spending and a 4% rate, that is 750,000 in today's money. The target is then grown with inflation for each future year.

faq.question: Does the tool account for taxes?
faq.answer: Not directly, because tax treatment differs by country and account type. The practical approach is to enter an after-tax expected return, or to add your expected tax bill to annual spending.

faq.question: What is sequence-of-returns risk?
faq.answer: It is the risk of a large market drop in the first years of retirement, when withdrawals are taken from a shrinking portfolio. Two retirees with identical average returns can end up with very different outcomes depending on the order in which those returns arrive. Cash buffers and flexible spending reduce the damage.

faq.question: Can I model a career break or a mortgage payoff?
faq.answer: Approximately. Run one projection up to the break, note the balance, then start a second projection with that balance as the starting capital and adjusted contributions. Full multi-phase modelling is planned for a later release.

tdee.name: TDEE & Macro Nutrition Calculator
tdee.metaTitle: TDEE Calculator — Daily Calories and Macronutrient Split
tdee.metaDescription: Calculate BMR and TDEE with the Mifflin-St Jeor or Katch-McArdle formula, then get calorie and macronutrient targets for cutting, maintenance or lean bulking. Metric and imperial units.
tdee.intro: Work out your basal metabolic rate, total daily energy expenditure and a protein-first macro split for your goal — in metric or imperial units.
features: Cut, maintain and lean-bulk calorie targets
BMI, lean body mass, fibre and water targets

ui.formulaFallback: Body fat % missing — Mifflin-St Jeor used instead.
ui.activityAthlete: Athlete — twice daily or physical job
ui.notMedicalAdvice: Estimates for healthy adults. Not medical advice — consult a professional before large dietary changes.

formula.intro: Total daily energy expenditure is basal metabolic rate multiplied by an activity factor, then adjusted for your goal. Which BMR formula is more accurate depends on whether you know your body-fat percentage.
steps: Mifflin-St Jeor (men): BMR = 10 × kg + 6.25 × cm − 5 × age + 5.
Mifflin-St Jeor (women): BMR = 10 × kg + 6.25 × cm − 5 × age − 161.
Katch-McArdle: BMR = 370 + 21.6 × lean body mass (kg), where LBM = weight × (1 − body fat%).
TDEE = BMR × activity factor (1.2 sedentary → 1.9 athlete).
Target calories = TDEE × (1 + goal adjustment), never below 90% of BMR.
Protein = g/kg from the chosen preset; fat = a share of total calories; carbohydrates fill the remainder (4/4/9 kcal per gram).
formula.note: Activity factors are population averages and can be off by 10–15% for an individual. Track your weight for two to three weeks and adjust calories by 100–200 until the trend matches your goal.

sections.heading: BMR, TDEE and why the difference matters
paragraphs: Basal metabolic rate is what your body burns doing nothing at all: heartbeat, breathing, temperature, brain. For most people it accounts for 60–70% of total daily energy use. Total daily energy expenditure adds the rest — planned exercise, everyday movement and the energy cost of digesting food.
Eating at BMR instead of TDEE is one of the most common dieting mistakes. It creates a deficit far larger than intended, which usually ends in muscle loss, fatigue and a rebound.

sections.heading: Choosing the right formula
paragraphs: Mifflin-St Jeor is the default recommendation for the general population and needs only height, weight, age and sex. Katch-McArdle works from lean body mass instead, which makes it more accurate for lean, muscular or very heavy individuals — but only if your body-fat estimate is reliable.

If your body-fat number comes from a cheap bioimpedance scale, treat it as a rough estimate and prefer Mifflin-St Jeor. DEXA, hydrostatic weighing or careful calliper measurements justify Katch-McArdle.

sections.heading: Setting protein, fat and carbohydrates
paragraphs: Protein is set first because it is the macronutrient most strongly linked to keeping muscle in a deficit and to satiety: roughly 1.6–2.2 g per kg of bodyweight for active people, and the upper end when cutting hard.

Fat should generally stay above about 0.6 g per kg to support hormone production, and carbohydrates take whatever calories remain — they are the cheapest fuel for hard training. A keto split inverts this, pushing fat to about 70% of calories and leaving carbohydrates minimal.
list: Protein: 4 kcal per gram, 1.6–2.4 g/kg depending on goal
Fat: 9 kcal per gram, 25–35% of calories in most splits
Carbohydrates: 4 kcal per gram, the remaining calories

sections.heading: How fast should the weight move?
paragraphs: A deficit of 500 kcal per day corresponds to roughly 0.45 kg per week, since about 7700 kcal is stored in a kilogram of body fat. Sustainable cutting usually means 0.5–1% of bodyweight per week; faster rates increase muscle loss.

For lean bulking the reverse applies: a surplus of 10% is usually enough to add tissue without excessive fat gain. Recalculate after every 3–4 kg of change, because both BMR and TDEE move with your bodyweight.

faq.question: How accurate is a TDEE calculator?
faq.answer: Formula-based estimates are typically within 10–15% of measured expenditure for healthy adults. Use the number as a starting point, then adjust based on two to three weeks of weight trend data rather than day-to-day fluctuation.

faq.question: Mifflin-St Jeor or Katch-McArdle?
faq.answer: Use Mifflin-St Jeor unless you have a reliable body-fat measurement. Katch-McArdle is based on lean body mass, which makes it better for athletic or very heavy bodies, but it inherits any error in your body-fat estimate.

faq.question: How much protein do I actually need?
faq.answer: For active adults, 1.6–2.2 g per kg of bodyweight covers almost all evidence-based recommendations. Aim for the upper end during a calorie deficit to protect muscle, and spread intake across three to five meals.

faq.question: Why did my weight not change even though I ate at the target?
faq.answer: Water retention, glycogen, sodium, menstrual cycle and food weight in the gut can mask fat loss for one to two weeks. Compare weekly averages instead of single mornings, and only change calories if the trend is flat for two to three weeks.

faq.question: Is it safe to eat below my BMR?
faq.answer: It is generally not advisable without medical supervision. The calculator floors your target at 90% of BMR for that reason. Very low intakes risk muscle loss, micronutrient deficiency, hormonal disruption and poor adherence.

faq.question: Do I need to recalculate as I lose weight?
faq.answer: Yes. BMR scales with bodyweight, so recalculate after every 3–4 kg of change, or roughly once a month during an active phase, to keep the deficit or surplus at the intended size.

compound.name: Compound Interest Calculator
compound.metaTitle: Compound Interest Calculator — Project Investment Growth
compound.metaDescription: Estimate how savings and monthly contributions grow with compound interest. Free tool with a year-by-year breakdown and a shareable result card.
compound.intro: See how reinvested returns accelerate wealth over time. Enter a starting amount, a monthly contribution and an annual return to project your balance year by year.

ui.futureValueHint: Projected balance at the end of the term
ui.interestRatio: Interest is {percent}% of the final value

steps: Start with your initial principal P.
Each compounding period, the balance earns the periodic rate r/n, then the periodic deposit is added.
Repeat for n compounding periods per year across all t years.
The final balance A is your future value; subtract total deposits to find the interest earned.
formula.intro: Compound interest means you earn returns on your returns. The more often interest compounds, the faster the balance grows.
formula.note: Figures are nominal and exclude taxes, fees and inflation. They are illustrative, not financial advice.

sections.heading: What is compound interest?
paragraphs: Compound interest is the process where the interest you earn is reinvested, so future interest is calculated on a larger balance.
Over long horizons this snowball effect dwarfs the impact of your original deposit.

sections.heading: How often should interest compound?
paragraphs: More frequent compounding (monthly vs. annually) produces slightly more growth because interest starts earning sooner.
Our calculator defaults to monthly compounding, the most common schedule for brokerage and retirement accounts.

sections.heading: Making the most of compounding
paragraphs: Start early — time is the single biggest lever on the final balance.
Contribute consistently and reinvest dividends to maximize the snowball.
Even modest monthly deposits compound into large sums over decades.

faq.question: What is the compound interest formula?
faq.answer: The future value combines the compounded principal P(1 + r/n)^(nt) with the compounded value of periodic deposits. Our calculator applies the rate each period and adds your deposit, repeating for every period across the full term.

faq.question: Does compounding frequency matter?
faq.answer: Yes, but modestly. Monthly compounding beats annual by a small margin because interest begins earning sooner. The calculator lets you compare schedules.

faq.question: Are my returns guaranteed?
faq.answer: No. The figures are deterministic projections using the rate you enter; real markets fluctuate and the result excludes taxes, fees and inflation.

faq.question: How do regular contributions help?
faq.answer: Consistent monthly deposits add new principal that then compounds, often contributing more to the final balance than the initial lump sum over long periods.

faq.question: Why does the balance grow faster later?
faq.answer: Because each period’s interest is calculated on a larger balance. The snowball accelerates as the compounded amount overtakes your contributions.

faq.question: Can I share or save my result?
faq.answer: Yes — use the shareable result card to download an SVG or copy a link that preserves your exact inputs.

mortgage.name: Mortgage & Amortization Calculator
mortgage.metaDescription: Estimate monthly principal & interest, total interest, payoff time and a full amortization schedule for a fixed-rate mortgage — with extra payments. All runs in your browser.
mortgage.intro: See your monthly payment, lifetime interest and payoff date at a glance. Enter a home price, down payment, term and rate — then add an extra monthly payment to see how fast you can own the home free and clear.
features: Total interest and total loan cost

steps: Start with the loan amount: home price minus down payment.
Divide the annual rate by 12 for a monthly rate r.
Monthly payment M = L·r / (1 − (1+r)^−n), where L is the loan and n is the number of months.
Each month interest = balance·r and the rest of the payment reduces principal; any extra payment goes 100% to principal.
formula.intro: A fixed-rate mortgage uses amortization: every payment is split between interest on the remaining balance and principal repayment. Early on, interest dominates; later, principal does — the schedule makes this visible year by year.
formula.note: Figures are principal & interest only. Property taxes, insurance and PMI are not included, and results are illustrative, not a loan offer.

sections.heading: What is amortization?
paragraphs: Amortization is the process of paying down a loan with equal monthly payments, where each payment covers the interest accrued on the remaining balance plus a portion of the principal.
Because the balance shrinks, the interest portion falls over time and the principal portion grows — the reason early payments feel like "all interest".

sections.heading: Should I pay off my mortgage early?
paragraphs: Extra monthly payments go straight to principal, which shortens the term and cuts total interest — often by tens of thousands of dollars.
Whether it is the best use of your cash depends on your rate versus the return you could earn elsewhere, but the calculator makes the trade-off concrete.

faq.question: How is my monthly mortgage payment calculated?
faq.answer: The payment is computed with the standard amortization formula: loan amount, monthly interest rate and term. It covers principal and interest only — taxes, insurance and PMI are separate.

faq.question: Why is so much of my early payment interest?
faq.answer: Each payment first covers interest on the remaining balance. Since the balance is largest at the start, early payments are mostly interest; as the balance falls, more of the payment goes to principal.

faq.question: How do extra payments help?
faq.answer: An extra monthly payment is applied 100% to principal. That reduces the balance faster, which cuts future interest and shortens the payoff term — the calculator shows both the months saved and the interest saved.

faq.question: What is included in total loan cost?
faq.answer: Total loan cost is the sum of every principal and interest payment over the life of the loan — the loan amount plus all interest paid. It excludes the down payment, taxes and insurance.

faq.question: Does a larger down payment change my payment?
faq.answer: Yes. A larger down payment means a smaller loan, which lowers the monthly payment and total interest. You can switch the input between a dollar amount and a percentage to compare.

faq.question: Can I save or share this result?
faq.answer: Yes — the share link carries your exact inputs, the result card can be downloaded as an image, and the year-by-year schedule exports to CSV.

body-fat-bmi.name: Body Fat & BMI Calculator
body-fat-bmi.metaTitle: Body Fat & BMI Calculator — Navy Method & Health Range
body-fat-bmi.metaDescription: Measure body fat percentage with the U.S. Navy method, calculate BMI, and see fat mass, lean mass and healthy ranges. All runs in your browser.
body-fat-bmi.intro: Two key health numbers from simple measurements. Enter gender, age, height, weight and neck, waist (and hip for women) circumference — the Navy method estimates body fat while BMI checks your weight band.

steps: Calculate BMI: weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared.
Convert height, waist, neck (and hip for women) to inches.
Male body fat % = 495 / (1.0324 − 0.19077·log10(waist−neck) + 0.15456·log10(height)) − 450.
Female body fat % = 495 / (1.29579 − 0.35004·log10(waist+hip−neck) + 0.22100·log10(height)) − 450.
formula.intro: The U.S. Navy circumference method estimates body fat from tape measurements, and BMI classifies weight against height. Neither requires a special device — just a tape measure and a scale.
formula.note: Tape estimates are approximate; body fat varies with hydration and measurement technique. Results are educational, not a medical diagnosis.

sections.heading: What is body fat percentage?
paragraphs: Body fat percentage is the share of your total weight made up of fat tissue. The rest — muscle, bone, organs and water — is your lean mass.
The U.S. Navy method estimates the percentage from circumferences, so you can track composition changes without a body-fat scale or impedance device.

sections.heading: BMI vs body fat: why both?
paragraphs: BMI is a quick weight-for-height screen, but it cannot tell muscle from fat — a muscular athlete can read "overweight" while carrying little fat.
Body fat percentage fills that gap. Checking both gives a more honest picture of your health and your progress.

faq.question: How is body fat percentage calculated here?
faq.answer: It uses the U.S. Navy circumference method with waist, neck and height (plus hip for women). Enter the measurements in metric or imperial and the estimate updates instantly.

faq.question: What is the U.S. Navy method?
faq.answer: A tape-measure body fat formula originally developed for military personnel. It uses logarithms of circumference differences to estimate fat percentage without electrical impedance.

faq.question: What is a healthy BMI?
faq.answer: WHO classes BMI under 18.5 as underweight, 18.5–24.9 as normal, 25–29.9 as overweight and 30+ as obese. BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnosis.

faq.question: What is a healthy body fat percentage?
faq.answer: Roughly 8–24% for men and 21–36% for women depending on age, with athletes at the lower end. The calculator shows the common band for your gender and age.

faq.question: Why do BMI and body fat disagree?
faq.answer: BMI only compares weight with height, so muscle counts the same as fat. Body fat percentage separates the two — that is why a fit person can have a high BMI but a healthy body fat reading.

faq.question: Can I save or share this result?
faq.answer: Yes — the share link carries your exact measurements, the result card downloads as an image, and the summary exports to CSV.
